title: AI-native SDLC: how the vendors compare

vendors.name: AWS
vendors.framework: AI-Driven Development Life Cycle, AI-DLC (Jul 2025; FS post May 2026)

vendors.name: OpenAI
vendors.framework: Building an AI-native engineering team (Codex guide, undated)

vendors.name: Microsoft
vendors.framework: Hypervelocity Engineering (HVE) Core for GitHub Copilot

anthropic.text: Six stages (Plan, Design, Build, Test, Deploy, Maintain) run as a loop, not a line. Stages are modular; adopt them in any order your dependencies allow.

aws.text: Three phases (Inception, Construction, Operations). Operations feeds production learning back into the next Inception cycle, so it is also a loop.

atlassian.text: Five workflow areas: Planning, Design, Development, Review, Maintenance. No dedicated Test or Deploy section, and not framed as a closed loop.

openai.text: Seven phases (Plan, Design, Build, Test, Review, Document, Deploy and maintain). Each phase splits work into what agents do and what engineers review or own.

microsoft.text: A working method rather than a lifecycle: Research, Plan, Implement, Review, supported by agents, prompts, instructions and skills.

github.text: No stage model. A platform for running multiple coding agents (Plan Mode, mission control, review, branch controls) on top of existing GitHub workflow.

anthropic.text: Each stage commits a named file (intent.md, spec.md, plan.md, the diff, review findings, incident record). The next stage starts by reading it. The commit chain is the audit trail.

aws.text: AI stores plans, requirements and design artifacts in the project repository so work continues across sessions. Artifact names are not standardised in the posts reviewed.

atlassian.text: Specs are versioned files in the repo. Design standards link to code and work items. Agent actions are written back to the system of record as an audit trail.

openai.text: A PLAN.md is committed to the codebase and AGENTS.md carries standing instructions. Fewer named artifacts than the Anthropic chain.

microsoft.text: The main page points to a separate AI Artifacts Architecture document rather than listing the artifacts.

github.text: Agents work through existing primitives: Git, pull requests and issues. The PR and issue thread is the record.

anthropic.text: CLAUDE.md for conventions, skills for policies applied consistently, hooks for rules that must always hold. All version controlled and reviewed like code.

aws.text: Steering files guide the agent on security policy, architecture standards, approved dependencies and regulatory guidance. Implemented through Amazon Q project rules and Kiro workflows.

atlassian.text: Teamwork Graph: a context engine joining 50+ sources (Jira, Confluence, Loom and others) with permissions enforced at the data layer. Design standards also live alongside code.

openai.text: AGENTS.md is included with every prompt and is used for documentation rules, test coverage and feedback loops such as running tests and linters.

microsoft.text: Instructions apply coding standards automatically; skills package reusable workflows. About 80 standards are bundled.

github.text: AGENTS.md rule files plus MCP servers from a GitHub MCP Registry guide agent behaviour.

anthropic.text: Hooks block or gate actions deterministically (protected paths, test-file edits, production deploys). Managed settings stop engineers switching them off.

aws.text: Enforcement is described mainly as automated quality gates in the CI/CD pipeline and steering files. No equivalent of per-action hooks appears in the posts reviewed.

atlassian.text: Platform leads centrally define, enforce and monitor standards. Agent loops are scoped and recorded. No per-action hook mechanism described.

openai.text: The guide mentions defining agent access scopes and permissions only. Codex sandbox and managed-config docs exist separately and were not reviewed.

microsoft.text: Not described on the pages reviewed.

github.text: An enterprise control plane lets admins set security policy, audit logging, access, allowed agents and model access. Branch controls govern when CI runs on agent code.

anthropic.text: Humans review at gates and judge intent and risk. Agentic review layers run first; human review is reserved for regulated and critical code.

links.label: AI in the PR review loop

aws.text: Humans validate each AI plan and decision before execution proceeds. The AI plans, asks clarifying questions, and implements only after human validation, repeated for every activity.

atlassian.text: Agents review first against shared standards; humans make the final judgement and keep accountability for quality and governance.

openai.text: Delegate, review, own: agents do the first review pass; engineers own architecture, final review and merge, and production sign-off.

microsoft.text: Stated principle: AI carries the rules, humans keep judgement, trade-offs, review and decisions.

github.text: Developer approves the plan before implementation; an automated first-pass review runs before a human sees agent code; mission control for steering.

anthropic.text: Autonomy is tiered by environment and risk. Agents act freely in dev, prepare the release in production, and a named person authorises it.

aws.text: Risk-based change categorisation: only material changes need human sign-off, routine changes flow through automated validation. Production and high-impact actions keep approval controls.

atlassian.text: No tiered or risk-based approval model described. Deploy is not addressed.

openai.text: Start with well-specified tasks and small review rollouts, then expand as results are trusted. Engineers retain sign-off on remediation.

microsoft.text: Not described on the pages reviewed.

github.text: Branch controls decide when CI and checks run on agent-created code. No explicit risk tiers in the post.

anthropic.text: Every session verifies its own work (tests, build, screenshot diff) before a human sees it. Continuous evals regression-test the agent configuration itself.

aws.text: AI validates its own work and self-corrects when tests fail, including deviations from steering files. QA is left-shifted, with high-fidelity test environments and security testing.

atlassian.text: Testing is mentioned briefly under Development. No feedback-loop or eval mechanism. An AI Reviewer checks gaps between requirements and what was built.

openai.text: Agents propose tests, ideally in a separate session from implementation. Engineers check for stubbed or shortcut tests. Feedback loops run tests and linters.

microsoft.text: A review agent exists; self-verification and evals are not described on the pages reviewed.

github.text: Quality is addressed through automated review and a Code Quality reporting preview. No agent self-verification loop described.

anthropic.text: Headless stage: a deterministic detector watches production metrics against control bands and invokes the agent, which writes the finding as a new intent.md. Scheduled security scans and Slack-based on-call extend it.

aws.text: Monitoring feeds the coding agent's context and informs future Inception cycles. AI agents (for example Amazon DevOps Agent) can investigate incident root causes. Less specific on autonomy tiers.

atlassian.text: Agents classify errors, draft root-cause analyses, handle routine fixes and dependency updates, and escalate. Work items are spawned from operational signals.

openai.text: Agents parse logs, flag suspect commits and propose hotfixes. Engineers validate the diagnosis and approve remediation. Teams are advised to run simulated incidents.

microsoft.text: Not described on the pages reviewed.

github.text: The post offers little on deploy or operations beyond agents running on Actions or self-hosted runners.

anthropic.text: Not prescribed. Focus is on artifacts, automation and gates. One engineer can run several parallel sessions, but no new team model or vocabulary is mandated.

aws.text: Prescriptive. AI Pods of 2 to 3 developers replace scrum teams of about 7. Sprints become "bolts", epics become Units of Work, and Mob Elaboration / Mob Construction are team rituals. Co-location matters in Inception.

atlassian.text: No detailed team model. Advises updating rituals, roles and success metrics alongside tooling. Designers and PMs can ship small UI changes and fixes via agents.

openai.text: No team model in the guide. Organised by phase and by who delegates, reviews or owns the work.

microsoft.text: Not described on the pages reviewed.

github.text: No team model. Mission control integrates with Slack, Teams, Jira, Linear and Azure Boards for assigning agent work.

anthropic.text: Each play names a leading and a lagging indicator, mostly read from git history, PR metadata and CI events (for example time from intent to spec, rework after build starts, DORA).

aws.text: A KPI suite (mean time to deploy and recover, failed-deployment %, incidents by severity, technical debt, NPS) plus Amazon's Cost-to-Serve-Software framework for the financial case.

atlassian.text: Build measurement before scaling. Uses DX to combine Jira, Cursor and Claude Code data with developer feedback. Track cost, productivity and ROI.

openai.text: Light signals: PR comment reactions, a gold-standard PR set to compare review tools, and whether agent commands succeed. No org-level KPI set.

microsoft.text: No outcome metrics. The page gives only repository statistics.

github.text: A Copilot metrics dashboard (public preview at announcement) reports usage and impact across an organisation.

anthropic.text: Dependency graph of twelve plays. Six have no prerequisites, so teams start anywhere and build up.

aws.text: Three-phase adoption: executive alignment, technical enablement, hands-on pilots. States mature DevSecOps must already exist, because AI-DLC amplifies existing capability.

atlassian.text: Five moves: connected permissioned context, early measurement, pick one starting stage and go deep, preserve accountability, build the operating model.

openai.text: Start with well-specified tasks, add guardrails, iterate on AGENTS.md, roll out review in small steps. A third-party summary adds a phased adoption timeline.

microsoft.text: Install as a VS Code extension or Copilot CLI plugin. Treat as a source of patterns, not a stable platform or production dependency.

github.text: Not addressed. The post describes planned capabilities.

anthropic.text: High. Step-by-step plays with example files, configs, prompts and governance notes for each play.

aws.text: Methodology and principles in the public posts, with the full method in a whitepaper (not yet reviewed here). Open-sourced workflows are available for implementation.

atlassian.text: Strategic with product examples. No file formats, configs or step-by-step plays.

openai.text: Per-phase tables and customer examples. Light on configs; hands-on detail sits in separate Codex docs.

microsoft.text: A usable starter kit of agents, prompts, instructions and skills rather than a methodology document.

github.text: A product announcement, not a methodology.

anthropic.text: No customer outcome figures in the playbook itself. It leans on Anthropic's internal practice and the measurement plays.

aws.text: Quotes figures: a Bedrock engine rebuilt by 6 engineers in 76 days against an estimate of 40 engineers for a year, and an unnamed European bank going from 12 to 3 developers. All vendor-reported.

links.label: A signal too big to ignore

atlassian.text: Internal figures: issue cycle time down from 11.5 to 6.7 days; agents with Teamwork Graph 44% more accurate with 48% fewer tokens; 51% of vulnerabilities auto-resolved. All vendor-reported.

openai.text: Customer examples (Cloudwalk, Sansan, Virgin Atlantic) and a claim that work once taking weeks now takes days. Few hard figures.

microsoft.text: None. The project itself cautions that it is evolving.

github.text: Platform statistics only (developer base and Copilot adoption). No delivery-outcome figures.

common.title: Plan before code
common.detail: Every vendor puts a written plan or spec ahead of implementation: intent, spec and plan files (Anthropic), Inception (AWS), versioned specs (Atlassian), a Plan phase (OpenAI), Research and Plan (Microsoft), Plan Mode (GitHub).

common.title: Humans keep judgement, agents do the first pass
common.detail: Agents plan, build and give first-pass review. People own intent, risk, final review and sign-off.

common.title: Rules are written down where the agent reads them
common.detail: CLAUDE.md and skills, steering files, AGENTS.md, instruction files. Atlassian does the same through a central context graph rather than repo files.

common.title: Measure the change
common.detail: Anthropic, AWS, Atlassian, OpenAI and GitHub all name some way to measure. Depth varies. Microsoft's repo gives no outcome metrics.

common.title: Start small, then expand
common.detail: Anthropic, AWS, Atlassian and OpenAI advise starting with one stage, pilot or well-specified task.

differences.title: How firmly rules are enforced
differences.detail: Anthropic describes deterministic enforcement (hooks, managed settings) and GitHub an admin control plane. AWS leans on pipeline gates and steering files. The rest say little.

differences.title: Team and operating model
differences.detail: Only AWS prescribes one: AI Pods, mob sessions, new vocabulary. Anthropic, OpenAI and GitHub leave team structure open.

differences.title: Closing the loop after release
differences.detail: Only Anthropic describes an autonomous loop where production signals become the next intent. AWS and Atlassian cover parts of it. OpenAI keeps engineers on sign-off. Microsoft and GitHub do not cover it.

differences.title: Where context lives
differences.detail: Anthropic, AWS, OpenAI and GitHub keep it in repo files. Atlassian builds a permissioned graph across Jira, Confluence and code.

differences.title: Evidence offered
differences.detail: AWS, Atlassian and OpenAI quote outcomes, all vendor-reported. Anthropic, Microsoft and GitHub give none for delivery results.

differences.title: Scope of the source
differences.detail: Anthropic and AWS publish methods. OpenAI publishes a guide. Atlassian skips Test and Deploy. Microsoft is a starter kit and GitHub a product announcement.

takeaway: Anthropic's playbook is the most implementable: strongest on enforceable controls, self-verification and closing the loop.
Others add what it lacks: AWS a team model and business case, Atlassian system-of-record context and measure-before-scaling, OpenAI a simple delegate, review, own framing.
The vendors agree on principles far more than on mechanics. Differences are mostly in enforcement, operating model and evidence.
